name: impacket
one_line: Python tools that speak Windows network protocols (SMB, Kerberos, RPC, LDAP)
plain: `impacket` is a collection of Python scripts for working with Windows and Active Directory protocols from Linux. On Kali they are installed as `impacket-NAME`, for example `impacket-smbclient` or `impacket-lookupsid`.

Most scripts take the target as `DOMAIN/USER:PASSWORD@HOST`. Instead of a password you can give an NT hash with `-hashes :NTHASH`, or a Kerberos ticket with `-k`. Pass `-h` to any script for its own options.
It is a defender's reference as much as an attacker's: seeing how each tool works shows what to detect. Run it only against machines you own or are allowed to test, such as a CTF or a home lab.
when: Enumerate a Windows host or domain from Linux in a lab.
Understand how a Windows protocol behaves by looking at the traffic it makes.
Use a credential you were given in a CTF against another service.
Practise Active Directory attack paths in your own lab, then write the detection.

examples.title: Browse a share
examples.explain: Opens an FTP-like prompt for SMB shares. Type `shares`, `use SHARE`, `ls`, `get FILE`.

examples.title: Look up accounts by SID
examples.explain: Counts up the numeric ids (RIDs) after the domain SID and prints the account names: a way to list users and groups.

examples.title: Which services use which ports
examples.explain: Lists the RPC endpoints a host exposes, to see what is running.

examples.title: Check a Kerberos setting
examples.explain: Asks the domain controller about accounts that do not require Kerberos pre-authentication (a misconfiguration). A lab exercise: the fix is to enable pre-auth, and the detection is repeated AS-REQ without pre-auth.

examples.title: Accounts with service names
examples.explain: Lists accounts that have service principal names. Adding -request fetches service tickets that can be tested for weak passwords offline: practise only in your lab, and read about the defence (long random service-account passwords, gMSA).

examples.title: Run a command with credentials you hold
examples.explain: Runs one command through WMI and prints the result. The same technique exists as impacket-psexec and impacket-smbexec; they differ in how noisy they are, which is what defenders look for.

examples.title: Use a hash instead of a password
examples.explain: Windows accepts the NT hash in place of the password for these protocols. This is why hash theft matters and why defenders limit where privileged accounts log in.

examples.title: A fake file share for a test
examples.explain: Starts an SMB server that shares ./loot. In a lab it is a quick way to move a file between two machines.

examples.title: Use a Kerberos ticket
examples.explain: -k uses the ticket named in KRB5CCNAME. Kerberos needs working DNS names and a clock within five minutes of the domain.

mistakes: Forgetting that Kerberos needs the right DNS names and a clock within five minutes.
Mixing up the script names: on Kali they are `impacket-NAME`; the older `NAME.py` form is the same script.
Trying a command on a host you are not authorised to test: this tool set is illegal outside a lab or an engagement.
Passing a password with special characters unquoted: wrap it in single quotes.
Running many guesses against accounts and locking them out: read the lockout policy first.
try: In a lab domain, list the users with impacket-lookupsid and compare with BloodHound.
Read the `-h` output for three scripts and explain what each protocol is.

see_also: smbclient(1), rpcclient(1), ldapsearch(1), bloodhound(1), nmap(1) (smb-*, ldap-* scripts), crackmapexec / netexec, evil-winrm, hashcat(1), john(1).
